title: Hands-On Exercise 2
section: Using the patchwork extension to create composite graphics
text:
Using the patchwork extension to create composite graphics
This extension is one of the ggplot2 extensions which is designed to combine separate ggplot2 graphs into single figure.
The general syntax that combines graphs are as follows:

2-column layout using the + sign
() to create a subplot group
2-row layout using the / sign


2 graphs combined
The code block below shows how 2 histograms are combined

p1 + p2










3 graphs combined
The code block below does the following to combine 3 plots:

/ stacks 2 ggplot2 graphs
| places the plots beside each other
() defines the sequence of the plotting


(p1 / p2) | p3

`geom_smooth()` using formula = 'y ~ x'











Creating the composite figure with tags
The package also provides auto-tagging capabilities to identify the subplots in the figure with plot_annotation().

((p1 / p2) | p3) + 
  plot_annotation(tag_levels = 'I')

`geom_smooth()` using formula = 'y ~ x'











Creating the composite figure with insert
The package also allows plots to be placed freely on top/below another plot with inset_element().

p3 + inset_element(p2, 
                   left = 0.02, 
                   bottom = 0.7, 
                   right = 0.5, 
                   top = 1)

`geom_smooth()` using formula = 'y ~ x'











Combining both patchwork and ggtheme while creating a composite figure
The code block showcases how both ggtheme and patchwork can be combined.

patchwork <- (p1 / p2) | p3
patchwork & theme_economist()

`geom_smooth()` using formula = 'y ~ x'

title: Hands-On Exercise 3
text:
The tooltip aesthetic
The following code chunks below plots the interactive statistical graph using the ggiraph pacakge. This performs the following:

ggplot() object is first created. along with geom_dotplot_interactive() where it generates an interactive version of the graph
girafe() is used to generate an svg object to be displayed on an html page


Tooltip with only Student’s ID

p <- ggplot(data=exam_data, 
       aes(x = MATHS)) +
  geom_dotplot_interactive(
    aes(tooltip = ID),
    stackgroups = TRUE, 
    binwidth = 1, 
    method = "histodot") +
  scale_y_continuous(NULL, 
                     breaks = NULL)
girafe(
  ggobj = p,
  width_svg = 6,
  height_svg = 6*0.618
)





When the mouse hovers over the points in the graph above, it will display the student’s ID. This is done by editing in the geom_dotplot_interactive() function, where aes(tooltip = ID).


Displaying multiple information using tooltip

exam_data$tooltip <- c(paste0(     
  "Name = ", exam_data$ID,         
  "\n Class = ", exam_data$CLASS)) 

p <- ggplot(data=exam_data, 
       aes(x = MATHS)) +
  geom_dotplot_interactive(
    aes(tooltip = exam_data$tooltip), 
    stackgroups = TRUE,
    binwidth = 1,
    method = "histodot") +
  scale_y_continuous(NULL,               
                     breaks = NULL)
girafe(
  ggobj = p,
  width_svg = 8,
  height_svg = 8*0.618
)





In this code block, where both the student’s ID and the class the student is in are to be displayed, a variable exam_data$tooltip is created in the first 3 lines of code, where it defines how it will be displayed. Afterwards, in the main body of code, tooltip is then assigned to exam_data$tooltip.


Customise your tooltip style

tooltip_css <- "background-color:white; #<<
font-style:bold; color:black;" #<<

p <- ggplot(data=exam_data, 
       aes(x = MATHS)) +
  geom_dotplot_interactive(              
    aes(tooltip = ID),                   
    stackgroups = TRUE,                  
    binwidth = 1,                        
    method = "histodot") +               
  scale_y_continuous(NULL,               
                     breaks = NULL)
girafe(                                  
  ggobj = p,                             
  width_svg = 6,                         
  height_svg = 6*0.618,
  options = list(    #<<
    opts_tooltip(    #<<
      css = tooltip_css)) #<<
)                                        





In this code block, the style is changed, where the background colour is while and the font colour and black and bolded.
This is done by introducing the variable tooltip_css, where you will assign the background colour, font style and the colour.
Afterwards, within the girafe() function, there is an additional options, where you would reference the tooltip_css as such there.


Advanced tooltip: displaying statistics
Let’s say that I want to display the 90% confidence interval of the mean of each subjects in the graph below.

tooltip <- function(y, ymax, accuracy = .01) {
  mean <- scales::number(y, accuracy = accuracy)
  sem <- scales::number(ymax - y, accuracy = accuracy)
  paste("Mean maths scores:", mean, "+/-", sem)
}

gg_point <- ggplot(data=exam_data, 
                   aes(x = RACE),
) +
  stat_summary(aes(y = MATHS, 
                   tooltip = after_stat(  
                     tooltip(y, ymax))),  
    fun.data = "mean_se", 
    geom = GeomInteractiveCol,  
    fill = "light blue"
  ) +
  stat_summary(aes(y = MATHS),
    fun.data = mean_se,
    geom = "errorbar", width = 0.2, size = 0.2
  )

Warning: Using `size` aesthetic for lines was deprecated in ggplot2 3.4.0.
ℹ Please use `linewidth` instead.

girafe(ggobj = gg_point,
       width_svg = 8,
       height_svg = 8*0.618)





In the code chunk above, tooltip is referenced in the first 4 lines, where the function is created to calculate the mean scores for the subjects with the intervals, along with how it is going to be displayed.
After that, it is then pointed within stat_summary() as shown in the code chunk.

title: Hands-On Exercise 3
text:
The data_id aesthetic
Let’s say, I want to identify visually the students in the same class over the histodot graph below.

p <- ggplot(data=exam_data, 
       aes(x = MATHS)) +
  geom_dotplot_interactive(           
    aes(data_id = CLASS),             
    stackgroups = TRUE,               
    binwidth = 1,                        
    method = "histodot") +               
  scale_y_continuous(NULL,               
                     breaks = NULL)
girafe(                                  
  ggobj = p,                             
  width_svg = 6,                         
  height_svg = 6*0.618                      
)                                        





What is done is that data_id is used within geom_dotplot_interactive() where it referenced CLASS (data_id = CLASS). As such, when the clicker hovers over the dots, the dots will change colour to orange, where it indicates the students that are in the same class. This allows me to visually see the distributions of the students.
It is to note that the default colour for this is orange, where: hover_css = "fill:orange;"

Re-styling the hover effect
Instead of the dot’s colour changing to orange, I would want to highlight the students that are in the same class.

p <- ggplot(data=exam_data, 
       aes(x = MATHS)) +
  geom_dotplot_interactive(              
    aes(data_id = CLASS),              
    stackgroups = TRUE,                  
    binwidth = 1,                        
    method = "histodot") +               
  scale_y_continuous(NULL,               
                     breaks = NULL)
girafe(                                  
  ggobj = p,                             
  width_svg = 6,                         
  height_svg = 6*0.618,
  options = list(                        
    opts_hover(css = "fill: #202020;"),  
    opts_hover_inv(css = "opacity:0.2;") 
  )                                        
)                                        





In the code block above, options is introduced within the girafe() function, where you can do the highlighting effect as such.

        data_id = CLASS),              
    stackgroups = TRUE,

  scale_y_continuous(NULL,               
                     breaks = NULL)
girafe(                                  
  ggobj = p,                             
  width_svg = 6,                         
  height_svg = 6*0.618,
  options = list(                        
    opts_hover(css = "fill: #202020;"),  
    opts_hover_inv(css = "opacity:0.2;")

The graph shows how the students in the same class is both highlighted, and shown as the tooltip.

title: Hands-On Exercise 3
text:
Coordinated Multiple Views
In hands-on exercise 2, we came across the use of multiple graphs. This can also be applied in interactive statistical graphs as well.
In this example, I will be displaying the graph of marks for both Maths and Science. When the mouse hovers over a data point in either graph, the corresponding data point on the other visualisation will be highlighted as well.
This is done by:

Using appropriate interactive functions of ggiraph to create the multiple views.
Using patchwork function within the girafe function to create the interactive coordinated multiple views.

The code chunk below showcases that.

p1 <- ggplot(data=exam_data, 
       aes(x = MATHS)) +
  geom_dotplot_interactive(              
    aes(data_id = ID),              
    stackgroups = TRUE,                  
    binwidth = 1,                        
    method = "histodot") +  
  coord_cartesian(xlim=c(0,100)) + 
  scale_y_continuous(NULL,               
                     breaks = NULL)

p2 <- ggplot(data=exam_data, 
       aes(x = ENGLISH)) +
  geom_dotplot_interactive(              
    aes(data_id = ID),              
    stackgroups = TRUE,                  
    binwidth = 1,                        
    method = "histodot") + 
  coord_cartesian(xlim=c(0,100)) + 
  scale_y_continuous(NULL,               
                     breaks = NULL)

girafe(code = print(p1 + p2), 
       width_svg = 6,
       height_svg = 3,
       options = list(
         opts_hover(css = "fill: #202020;"),
         opts_hover_inv(css = "opacity:0.2;")
         )
       ) 





The data_id aesthetic is critical to link observations between both plots, while the tooltip aesthetic is optional but a nice to have to improve the visualisation.

title: Hands-On Exercise 3
text:
Coordinated Multiple Views with plotly
To create a coordinated linked plot using plotly, 3 steps need to be done:

highlight_key() of plotly is used as shared data
2 scatterplots will be created using ggplot2 functions
`subplot() of plotly is used to place them next to each other side-by-side


d <- highlight_key(exam_data)
p1 <- ggplot(data=d, 
            aes(x = MATHS,
                y = ENGLISH)) +
  geom_point(size=1) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim=c(0,100),
                  ylim=c(0,100))

p2 <- ggplot(data=d, 
            aes(x = MATHS,
                y = SCIENCE)) +
  geom_point(size=1) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim=c(0,100),
                  ylim=c(0,100))
subplot(ggplotly(p1),
        ggplotly(p2))





It is to note that highlight_key() simply creates an object of class crosstalk::SharedData.

title: Hands-On Exercise 4
text:
Distribution with Ridgeline Plot
A ridgeline plot (or Joyplot) is a technique of data visualisation that reveals the distribution of a numeric value for several groups. The distributions can be represented by using either histograms or density plots, all alligned to the same horizontal scale and presented with a slight overlap.
When are ridgeline plots applicable in explaining our data findings?

They make sense when the number of groups to represent is medium to high, so often a classic window separation takes too much space. When groups overlap each other, it allows the use of space more efficiently. However, if there is < than 5 groups, other forms of distribution plots would be better.
They make sense when there is a clear pattern in the result (i.e. obvious ranking in groups). Else, the groups will overlap one another, leading to a messy plot, making it counter-intuitive.


Plotting the ridgeline with the ggridges method
The ggridges package is one of the ways to build a ridgeline plot. In the package, it provides 2 main geom to do so:

geom_ridgeline(): This function takes height values directly to draw the ridgelines
geom_density_ridges(): This function first estimates the data densities and then draws those using ridgelines

The code chunk below is plotted using geom_density_ridges():

ggplot(exam_data, 
       aes(x = ENGLISH, 
           y = CLASS)) +
  geom_density_ridges(
    scale = 3,
    rel_min_height = 0.01,
    bandwidth = 3.4,
    fill = lighten("#7097BB", .3),
    color = "white"
  ) +
  scale_x_continuous(
    name = "English Grades",
    expand = c(0, 0)
    ) +
  scale_y_discrete(name = NULL, expand = expansion(add = c(0.2, 2.6))) +
  theme_ridges()










Making the plot more colourful along the x-axis
At times, we would like the area under the ridgelines to be filled with colours that vary in some form along the x-axis. This is achieved by using either geom_ridgeline_gradient() or geom_density_ridges_gradient(). Both functions acts the same as the functions discussed earlier, only with the added effect of varying fill colours. However, they do not allow for alpha transparency in the fill, therefore a choice have to be made: have changing fill colours or transparency.
The code chunk below showcases the effect:

ggplot(exam_data, 
       aes(x = ENGLISH, 
           y = CLASS,
           fill = stat(x))) +
  geom_density_ridges_gradient(
    scale = 3,
    rel_min_height = 0.01) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(name = "Temp. [F]",
                       option = "C") +
  scale_x_continuous(
    name = "English Grades",
    expand = c(0, 0)
  ) +
  scale_y_discrete(name = NULL, expand = expansion(add = c(0.2, 2.6))) +
  theme_ridges()

Warning: `stat(x)` was deprecated in ggplot2 3.4.0.
ℹ Please use `after_stat(x)` instead.


Picking joint bandwidth of 3.18











Mapping probabilities directly onto colour
The package also provides a statistic function, called stat_density_ridges() that replaces stat_density() of ggplot2. This function plots the ridgeline by mapping the probabilities calculated via the use of stats(ecdf).
The code chunk below uses the function above, which represents the empirical cumulative density function for the distribution of English score.

ggplot(exam_data,
       aes(x = ENGLISH, 
           y = CLASS, 
           fill = 0.5 - abs(0.5-stat(ecdf)))) +
  stat_density_ridges(geom = "density_ridges_gradient", 
                      calc_ecdf = TRUE) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(name = "Tail probability",
                       direction = -1) +
  theme_ridges()

Picking joint bandwidth of 3.18









NOTE: You must include the argument calc_ecdf = TRUE in stat_density_ridges().


Plotting ridgelines quantile-ly
The function geom_density_ridges_gradient() also allows the plot to be coloured by quantile, via the calculated stats(quantile)aesthetic as shown in the figure below.

ggplot(exam_data,
       aes(x = ENGLISH, 
           y = CLASS, 
           fill = factor(stat(quantile))
           )) +
  stat_density_ridges(
    geom = "density_ridges_gradient",
    calc_ecdf = TRUE, 
    quantiles = 4,
    quantile_lines = TRUE) +
  scale_fill_viridis_d(name = "Quartiles") +
  theme_ridges()

Picking joint bandwidth of 3.18









We can also specify specific quartiles by cut points like 2.5% or 97.5% tails to colour the plot as shown below.

ggplot(exam_data,
       aes(x = ENGLISH, 
           y = CLASS, 
           fill = factor(stat(quantile))
           )) +
  stat_density_ridges(
    geom = "density_ridges_gradient",
    calc_ecdf = TRUE, 
    quantiles = c(0.025, 0.975)
    ) +
  scale_fill_manual(
    name = "Probability",
    values = c("#FF0000A0", "#A0A0A0A0", "#0000FFA0"),
    labels = c("(0, 0.025]", "(0.025, 0.975]", "(0.975, 1]")
  ) +
  theme_ridges()

Picking joint bandwidth of 3.18

title: Hands-On Exercise 4
text:
Distribution using Raincloud Plot
Another data visualisation technique for data distribution would be Raincloud Plot, which produces a half-density to a distribution plot. As the name suggests, the density plot is in the shape of a “raincloud”. This plot enhances the traditional box-plot by highlighting multiple modalities (an indication that groups may exists). A boxplot does not show where the densities are clustered, but a raincloud plot does.
In this part of the exercise, we will be visualising the distribution of English score by race by using the raincloud plot. It will be created by using functions provided by ggdist and ggplot2 packages.

Plot a Half Eye Graph
To plot this graph, we are using the function stat_halfeye() of the ggdist package. This produces the visualisation, which contains a half-density and a slab-interval.

ggplot(exam_data, 
       aes(x = RACE, 
           y = ENGLISH)) +
  stat_halfeye(adjust = 0.5,
               justification = -0.2,
               .width = 0,
               point_colour = NA)








In the code chunk above, the slab interval is removed by setting .width = 0 and point_colour = NA.


Adding boxplot with geom_boxplot()
We will add the second geometry layer by using the function geom_boxplot() of ggplot2. This will produce a narrow boxplot. We will then reduce the width and adjust the opacity.

ggplot(exam_data, 
       aes(x = RACE, 
           y = ENGLISH)) +
  stat_halfeye(adjust = 0.5,
               justification = -0.2,
               .width = 0,
               point_colour = NA) +
  geom_boxplot(width = .20,
               outlier.shape = NA)










Adding Dot Plots with stat_dots()
We will add the third geometry layer by using the function stats_dots() of the ggdist package. This will produce a half-dot plot, similar to a histograph that indicates the number of samples (number of dots) in each bin. side = "left" is written to indicate that we cant it on the left-hand side.

ggplot(exam_data, 
       aes(x = RACE, 
           y = ENGLISH)) +
  stat_halfeye(adjust = 0.5,
               justification = -0.2,
               .width = 0,
               point_colour = NA) +
  geom_boxplot(width = .20,
               outlier.shape = NA) +
  stat_dots(side = "left", 
            justification = 1.2, 
            binwidth = .5,
            dotsize = 2)










Finishing it up
The last geometric layer is to use the function coord_flip() of the ggplot2 package. This flips the raincloud chart horizontally to give it the “raincloud’ experience. theme_economist() of the ggthemes package is also added to give the raincloud chart a professional publishing standard look.

ggplot(exam_data, 
       aes(x = RACE, 
           y = ENGLISH)) +
  stat_halfeye(adjust = 0.5,
               justification = -0.2,
               .width = 0,
               point_colour = NA) +
  geom_boxplot(width = .20,
               outlier.shape = NA) +
  stat_dots(side = "left", 
            justification = 1.2, 
            binwidth = .5,
            dotsize = 1.5) +
  coord_flip() +
  theme_economist()

One-sample test: The gghistostats() method
The code chunk below shows how gghistostats() is used to build a visual of one-sample test on English scores.

set.seed(1234)

gghistostats(
  data = exam_data,
  x = ENGLISH,
  type = "bayes",
  test.value = 60,
  xlab = "English scores"
)








The following information is given from the test:

Statistical details

Sample sizes
Distribution summary


What is Bayes Factor?
Bayes Factor is a measure of the strength of evidence in favour of one hypothesis among two competing hypotheses. This offers a way to evaluate the data in favour of a null hypothesis (H0) & use external information to do so. It also tells us the weight of the evidence in favour of a given hypothesis.
when comparing both alternative (H1) and null (H0) hypotheses, the factor often written as B10. This is defined as follows:
\[
\frac{\text{likelihood of data given } H_1}
{\text{likelihood of data given } H_0}
=
\frac{P(D \mid H_1)}
{P(D \mid H_0)}
\]
The Schwarz criterion is one of the easiest ways to calculate rough approximation of the Bayes Factor.


Interpreting Bayes Factor
The ratio of the factor is positive. Below is a table of common interpretation of the values of the Bayes Factor:



If B10 is…
Then you have…




> 100
Extreme evidence for H1


30 - 100
Very strong evidence for H1


10 - 30
Strong evidence for H1


3 - 10
Moderate evidence for H1


1 - 3
Anecdotal evidence for H1


1
No evidence


1/3 - 1
Anecdotal evidence for H0


1/10 - 1/3
Moderate evidence for H0


1/30 - 1/10
Strong evidence for H0


1/100 - 1/30
Very strong evidence for H0


< 1/100
Extreme evidence for H0

text:
Visualising the uncertainty of point estimates using ggplot2
A point estimate is a single number, like mean. Uncertainty is expressed as a standard error, like confidence interval. Uncertainty of a point estimate IS NOT EQUAL to the variance of a sample!
In this section, we will be plotting error bars of Maths scores by race by using data provided in the exam_data tibble dataframe.
First, the code chunk below will derive the necessary summary statistics:

my_sum <- exam_data %>%
  group_by(RACE) %>%
  summarise(
    n=n(),
    mean=mean(MATHS),
    sd=sd(MATHS)
    ) %>%
  mutate(se=sd/sqrt(n-1))

From the code chunk above:

group_by() of the dplyr package is used to group the observation by race
summarise() is used to compute the count, mean and standard deviation of the observations
mutate() is used to derive standard error of Maths by race
The output is then sabled as a tibble data table called my_sum

Next, the code chunk below is used to display my_sum tibble data frame in a HTML table format.

Plotting Standard Error bars of Point Estimates
The code chunk below provides the visualisation of the standard error bars of the mean Math score by race.

ggplot(my_sum) +
  geom_errorbar(
    aes(x=RACE, 
        ymin=mean-se, 
        ymax=mean+se), 
    width=0.2, 
    colour="black", 
    alpha=0.9, 
    linewidth=0.5) +
  geom_point(aes
           (x=RACE, 
            y=mean), 
           stat="identity", 
           color="red",
           size = 1.5,
           alpha=1) +
  ggtitle("Standard error of mean Maths score by race")








From the code chunk above:

Error bars are computed bt using the formula mean+/-se
It is important to indicate stat = "identity in the function geom_point()



Plotting Cofidence Interval of Point Estimates
We can also plot CIs of mean Maths scores by race with the following code chunk below:

ggplot(my_sum) +
  geom_errorbar(
    aes(x=reorder(RACE, -mean), 
        ymin=mean-1.96*se, 
        ymax=mean+1.96*se), 
    width=0.2, 
    colour="black", 
    alpha=0.9, 
    linewidth=0.5) +
  geom_point(aes
           (x=RACE, 
            y=mean), 
           stat="identity", 
           color="red",
           size = 1.5,
           alpha=1) +
  labs(x = "Maths score",
       title = "95% Confidence Interval of mean Maths score by Race")








From the code chunk:

CIs are computed using the formula mean+/-1.96*se
Error bars are sorted by using the average Math scores
labs() is used to change the label of the x-axis



Combining interactive error bars with the table
The code chunk below shows how the error bars become interactive, with the addition of the table for visualisation.

                     colour="black", 
                     alpha=0.9, 
                     size=0.5) +
                   geom_point(aes(
                     x=RACE, 
                     y=mean, 
                     text = paste("Race:", `RACE`, 
                                  "<br>N:", `n`,
                                  "<br>Avg. Scores:", round(mean, digits = 2),
                                  "<br>95% CI:[", 
                                  round((mean-2.58*se), digits = 2), ",",

                     stat="identity",

Visualising Uncertainty with ggdist
This package provides a flexible set of ggplot2 geoms and stats that are designed especially for visualising distributions and uncertainty.
This is designed for both frequentist and Bayesian uncertainty visualisation, with the view that such visualisation can be unified through the perspective of distribution visualisation.

Fequentist Models: One visualises confidence distributions or bootstrap distributions
Bayesian Models: One visualises probability distributions


Using ggdist to visualise uncertainty of point estimates
The code chunk below uses the function stats_pointinterval() of ggdist to build a visual to display distribution of the Math score by race.

exam_data %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = RACE, 
             y = MATHS)) +
  stat_pointinterval() +
  labs(
    title = "Visualising confidence intervals of mean math score",
    subtitle = "Mean Point + Multiple-interval plot")








This function comes with multiple arguments, therefore a read-up of the syntax reference would be strongly advised.

.width = 0.95

  stat_pointinterval(.width = 0.95,
  .point = median,
  .interval = qi) +
  labs(
    title = "Visualising confidence intervals of median math score",
